title: Prayer: A Bible Study on Learning to Pray
subtitle: A five-session study on prayer, walking slowly through the words Jesus gave us.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have been praying for years and quietly suspect they have never learned how, and for those who have stopped praying because the words ran out or the heavens went silent. It walks through the prayer Jesus taught when his own followers, who had watched him pray, asked him to teach them. Not a book on prayer. A school of prayer, run on the words of the Lord's Prayer itself, one clause at a time. Who we pray to and dare to call Father. What we are really asking when we ask for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come. The daily bread that ends our pretending we feed ourselves. The forgiveness we receive and the forgiveness we are bound to extend. And the prayer prayed in the dark, when the asking goes unanswered and the only faithful thing left is to keep asking anyway.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a technique for getting God to perform. It will refuse that, and the leader must refuse it too. Prayer is not a lever. It is a child speaking to a Father, and some in the room have no working picture of a father at all, because theirs left, or never came, or stayed and wounded. Bell knows that pew. He was raised without a father. He came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith to lean on and every reason to doubt the word Father meant anything. He is not standing outside this study explaining prayer to people who struggle with it. He is one of them. He has prayed into a ceiling. He has gone months saying the right words to a God who felt absent. He writes from inside the silence, and the leader will lead from there too.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Our Father
sessions.aim: To begin where Jesus begins, not with a method but with a name, and to face honestly that the first word of the prayer is the hardest word in it for anyone whose father failed them, while refusing both the sentimental picture of God and the bitter conclusion that the word means nothing.
sessions.summary: The disciples did not ask Jesus to teach them theology. They asked him to teach them to pray, and the first thing out of his mouth was a relationship, not a rule. Our Father. The first question of this whole study is not how to pray but to whom, because everything else depends on it. Bell takes the strong form of the wound. For the person whose father walked out, or never showed, or showed up only to do damage, the word Father is not warm. It is a closed door. He grants that completely, because he lived it. He was raised without a father and came to God from atheism, with no reason to expect the word would mean anything. But the answer is not to discard the word, which leaves you praying to a force, and it is not to pretend your earthly father was fine, which is a lie God never asked you to tell. Jesus is not saying God is like your father. He is saying God is the Father your father was always a broken copy of, the original your earthly one fell short of, the standard and not the echo. Then the turn. The word is our, not my, and it is in heaven, not at a safe distance. We come together, as children, to a Father who is both near enough to be addressed as Dad and high enough to be holy. The prayer begins by giving the fatherless a Father, which means the first thing prayer does is not change God. It tells you who you are.

keyScripture.why: Jesus opens the model prayer not with a request or a rule but with an address, our Father in heaven, naming the relationship before the asking and grounding all of prayer in adoption rather than technique, near enough to be called Father and high enough to be hallowed.

discussion.q: When you hear the word Father used of God, what is your honest first reaction, before the theologically correct one, and where do you think that reaction comes from?
discussion.behind: Surface the gut response before any teaching. For some the word is warm, for some it is a closed door, and the difference usually traces straight back to a human father. The aim is not to settle it but to expose it, because everyone in the room is praying to whatever picture that word calls up. Land it on honesty, and go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: The disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, and he answered first with a name and not a method. Why do you think he started with who we pray to rather than how?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the technique reflex. We come wanting a how, and Jesus gives a whom. The aim is to feel that prayer is grounded in a relationship before it is shaped by any rule, so the rest of the study is not a set of skills but a conversation with a Father.

discussion.q: Bell says God is not like your father, God is the Father your father was a broken copy of. What changes when you hear it that way around, the original instead of the echo?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge for the wounded. Many quietly assume God is their earthly father scaled up, which is terror for some. Help them feel the reversal, that the human father was the imperfect copy and God is the standard, so the failures of the one do not define the other. Handle tenderly.

discussion.q: Jesus says our Father, not my Father, and in heaven, not nearby and tame. How do those two words, our and in heaven, keep prayer from becoming either lonely or too casual?
discussion.behind: Get the room to hold both poles. Our makes prayer a family act, never a solo performance. In heaven keeps the Father holy and not a buddy. The aim is to feel prayer as intimate and reverent at once, addressed to one near enough to call Father and high enough to be hallowed.

discussion.q: Bell admits he came to God from atheism with no working picture of a father and has prayed into a ceiling more than once. Where have you found the word Father hard, and what have you done with that difficulty?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. You are not hunting for painful confession to display it. You want each person, the leader included, inside the difficulty, because the gospel gives a Father precisely to those who never had one. Go first, and keep it gentle.

objections.objection: Calling God Father is fine for people who had good fathers. For the rest of us it is a cruelty. You are asking me to feel safe with the very word that names the person who hurt me most, and no amount of theology fixes that.
objections.response: Sit inside this, because Bell does, and he will not answer it from a safe distance. He was raised without a father. He knows the word can land like a wound and not a comfort, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. So hear the distinction with care. Jesus is not saying God is a bigger version of your father. He is saying the reverse. God is the Father, the real and original one, and every earthly father, the absent one and the cruel one and even the good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken copy at that. Your father did not define fatherhood and then God had to live up to it. God defined it, and your father fell short. So when you pray our Father, you are not handing God the face of the man who failed you. You are appealing past that man to the One he was supposed to image and did not. The word does not belong to your wound. It belongs to God, and he is giving it to you.

objections.objection: If I have to feel a warm father-love to pray this honestly, I cannot do it, because I feel nothing toward the idea of God as Father. So either I am disqualified or I have to fake an emotion I do not have.
objections.response: You are not disqualified, and you are not asked to fake anything. Prayer does not begin with a feeling you generate. It begins with a fact you are given, that in Christ you have been adopted, made a child of God whether or not it feels true on a given morning. Bell came to God from atheism with no inherited warmth toward the word at all, and he prayed anyway, into a ceiling some nights, because the relationship is grounded in what God did and not in what we manage to feel. Romans says the Spirit himself cries Father in us when we cannot, that even our groaning is taken up and prayed. So pray the word before you feel it. Say Father as a child learning a name he did not grow up hearing, and let the feeling, if it comes, come later. The fact carries the prayer when the feeling cannot.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God really is the Father your earthly father was only a broken copy of, what is the one thing you have always wanted to hear a father say, and have never heard?
sessions.practice: This week, pray only the first two words. Our Father. Do not rush past them to the requests. Each day, say them slowly, several times, and notice what rises in you when you do, whether it is warmth, or nothing, or a flinch. Do not judge what comes. If the word is hard, say it anyway, as a child learning a name, and write down at the end of the week whether saying it changed how the rest of your prayers felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us say that word easily and some of us say it with a clenched jaw, because the man it should have named let us down or was never there at all. You know which of us is which. We thank you that you are not the echo of our earthly fathers but the original they failed to copy, and that you have made us your children not because we earned it but because you chose us. Teach the fatherless among us, and we are more of us than we admit, that they have a Father in heaven. Hallowed be your name. Amen.
reflection: What picture of a father do I bring to God without realizing it, and how has that picture shaped the way I pray, or kept me from praying at all?
Where have I assumed God is my earthly father scaled up, when Scripture says my earthly father was only ever a broken copy of him?
If I am truly adopted, a child of God whether or not it feels true today, what would change about how I come to him this week?
sessions.teaching: Start with the request that began it all. The disciples had watched Jesus pray, slipping away before dawn, praying through whole nights, praying with an intimacy and a power they had never seen, and one of them finally said, teach us to pray. Not teach us about prayer. Teach us to pray, the way John taught his disciples. And notice what Jesus does not do. He does not hand them a method, a posture, a breathing pattern, a list of techniques. He hands them a relationship, in the first word out of his mouth. Our Father. Before there is a single request, before kingdom or bread or forgiveness, there is an address, and the address is the whole foundation, because the first question of prayer was never how. It was always to whom. Everything depends on who is on the other end of the words. Now take the hardest objection at full strength, because it is the honest one, and for a great many people in any room it is not theoretical. Calling God Father is a comfort if you had a good father. It is a wound if you did not. For the person whose father walked out, or never appeared, or appeared only to do damage, the word Father is not a warm room. It is a locked door, and to be told to pray that word is to be told to feel safe with the name of the person who taught them that men leave. I will not wave that away, and I cannot, because I am that person. I was raised without a father. I came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith and no working picture of what a good father even was, and every reason to suspect the word was empty. So when I say I understand the flinch, I am not performing empathy. I am telling you my own. But here is what I learned, slowly, and it changed everything. Jesus is not saying God is like your father. That is the lie that terrifies the wounded, the assumption that God is simply your earthly father scaled up to cosmic size, the same absence and the same temper with more power behind it. Jesus is saying the exact opposite, and you have to hear the direction of it. God is the Father. The original. The real one. And every human father who ever lived, the one who left and the one who stayed and even the rare good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken copy at that. Your father did not set the standard for fatherhood that God then had to meet. God set the standard, and your father fell short of it, the way every image falls short of the original it was made from. This is not word play. It is the reversal the fatherless need most. When you pray our Father, you are not addressing the man who failed you with a bigger title. You are appealing past him, over his head, to the One he was supposed to show you and did not. The word does not belong to your wound. It belongs to God, and the staggering thing about the gospel is that he hands it to you anyway, hands the name Father to the very people who never got to use it. Then look at the two words wrapped around it, because they hold the whole thing in balance. It is our Father, not my Father. Jesus will not let prayer be a private performance, a solitary transaction between me and God. It is a family word. Even when you pray alone in a room, you pray as one of a people, joined to every other child crying the same name, which means the loneliest pray-er in the room is not alone. And it is our Father in heaven, not our Father down the hall, not a tame and chummy deity at our beck. In heaven keeps him holy. It means the One near enough to be called Father is also high enough to be hallowed, transcendent, the Lord of hosts, and the prayer holds both at once, intimacy and reverence in a single breath. Tim Keller used to say that if you have the fatherhood of God without the heaven, you get sentimentality, a God too soft to save you, a grandfather in the sky who indulges and never confronts, and if you have the heaven without the fatherhood, you get terror, a God too far and too high to reach, a judge who weighs and never welcomes. Jesus gives both, in a single breath, and you need both, because a Father who is not in heaven cannot rescue you and a holiness that is not your Father cannot comfort you. The wounded heart usually swings to one extreme or the other. It either makes God small and safe and manageable, a divine indulgence that asks nothing, or it makes him a towering threat, the absent father with infinite power, and neither of those is the God of this prayer. The God of this prayer is near enough to be addressed as Dad and high enough that his name is hallowed, and holding the two together is the work of a lifetime. And here is the verdict that should land before we ask for anything. The first thing prayer does is not change God's mind. It tells you who you are. Before you bring him a single need, he has already named you. Child. So if you came tonight not sure you have any standing to pray, not sure the word Father means anything when you say it, hear this. The standing was never yours to earn. It was given, in Christ, who made the fatherless into sons and daughters. Pray the word before you feel it. Say Father like a child learning a name he never got to use, and let the One who is the original, the real Father, the standard your father was only a shadow of, teach you slowly what the word was always meant to mean.

scriptureStudy.note: When you pray, say our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. The address comes first, before any request. Prayer is grounded in relationship, and the relationship is family, near enough for Father and high enough for hallowed.

Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples. They had watched him pray and wanted what he had. Notice the request is to be taught, which means prayer is learned, and even the disciples did not assume they already knew how.

You received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The right to call God Father is not natural, it is given in adoption, and the Spirit himself prompts the cry, so even the word in our mouths is grace.

God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The intimacy is the Spirit's work, not our achievement, which means the fatherless can pray the word truly because it is God's Spirit, not our history, that supplies it.

A father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. Long before Jesus, God claimed the title precisely for those who had no father, which tells you the name was always aimed at the ones who needed it most.

While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran. The father of the prodigal is Jesus' own picture of God the Father, who runs toward the returning child, the opposite of the distant or punishing father many fear.

See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God, and so we are. The adoption is not a metaphor stretched thin, it is a real new standing, named by the Father himself over those who had none.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian wrestling with how we can call God Father at all, because the word is more carefully weighted than the sentimental modern use of it suggests. The early church guarded the address fiercely. In many ancient liturgies the Lord's Prayer was taught only to the baptized, prayed for the first time at the moment of entering the family, because to call God Father was understood to be the unique privilege of the adopted, not the natural right of every creature. Set that beside the reflexive assumption of much modern religion that everyone everywhere is automatically a child of God in the same sense, and ask what is gained and what is lost in the flattening. The older view took adoption seriously as a gift, which made the word Father precious rather than generic. A serious group should also weigh the recovery, in writers like Keller and others drawing on the Reformers, of the doctrine of adoption as the high point of salvation, not merely forgiven but received into the family, not merely acquitted but named. And weigh the pastoral edge carefully, because here the doctrine meets the wound. For the fatherless, adoption is not an abstraction but the very thing they most lacked and most longed for, and the gospel offers it not as consolation prize but as the center, a Father deliberately given to those who had none, which is why Psalm 68 calls God the father of the fatherless before the New Testament ever opens. The discipline is to hold the word Father as both holy and tender, neither so reverent it goes cold nor so familiar it goes cheap, and to remember that for many in the room it is the most contested word in the prayer.

memoryVerse.text: Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.

sessions.title: Hallowed Be Your Name, Your Kingdom Come
sessions.aim: To see that the first things Jesus teaches us to ask for are not our needs but God's honor and God's reign, and that this ordering is not God's vanity but the cure for ours, prayer as the slow reordering of a disordered heart toward what is actually worth wanting.
sessions.summary: We come to prayer with a list, and our list starts with us. Jesus teaches a prayer where the first three petitions are about God, his name, his kingdom, his will, and only then turns to our bread. The first question is why. Why does the Father who already knows what we need make us ask first for his name to be honored, as though God were fishing for compliments. Bell takes the strong form of the suspicion, that a God who demands to be praised first sounds insecure, a cosmic ego needing applause before he attends to the help we actually came for. He grants how it sounds. But the suspicion misreads what hallowing is for. God does not need his name honored. We need to honor it, because a heart that puts anything else first is a heart already breaking on the wrong center. To pray hallowed be your name is not to flatter God. It is to ask him to retrain my wanting, to make first in me what is actually first in reality. Then your kingdom come, which is not a request for a better version of my plans but a prayer for a different king, the surrender of my small kingdom where I rule badly to the one kingdom that heals. Brueggemann would call it the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept that the way things are is the way they must be. The turn is this. Prayer is not first about getting what I want. It is about being given new wants. Desire reordered. The kingdom sought before the bread, the name hallowed before the need.

keyScripture.why: Hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven, placing God's honor, reign, and will ahead of every human request and naming prayer as the reordering of desire toward what is first in reality rather than first on our list.

discussion.q: Be honest about your own prayers. When you pray, what tends to come first, God's name and kingdom, or your needs and wants, and what does the order reveal?
discussion.behind: Open by exposing our default order before judging it. Most of us begin with our list, and naming that honestly is the start. The aim is not guilt but recognition, that Jesus reverses the order we naturally use, and the reversal is the point of the session.

discussion.q: Bell takes the suspicion seriously, that a God who wants to be praised first sounds insecure. What is true in that instinct, and how does it misread what hallowing is actually for?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The instinct rightly recoils from a needy God. The miss is that hallowing is not for God's benefit but for ours, the retraining of a heart that breaks when it centers on anything else. Help the room move from God needs praise to we need to praise.

discussion.q: To pray hallowed be your name is to ask God to make first in you what is actually first in reality. Where in your life is something other than God sitting in the first place, and how is that working out?
discussion.behind: Press gently on disordered desire. We all enthrone something, money, approval, a person, control, and call it normal. The aim is honest recognition of the wrong center, not a competition of confessions, so people feel why the petition is mercy and not vanity.

discussion.q: Your kingdom come is a prayer for a different king, which means surrendering the small kingdom where you rule. What does your kingdom, the one you run, look like, and what would it cost to pray for it to be replaced?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the cost. We all run a small kingdom and defend it. Praying your kingdom come is treason against our own rule. Help them name the kingdom they protect, and feel that this petition is not safe, it asks God to take the throne we have been sitting on.

discussion.q: Bell admits he prays your kingdom come while quietly hoping God will fund his kingdom instead. Where do you ask God to bless your plans rather than asking him to replace them with his?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Most of our kingdom-prayers are requests for divine sponsorship of our own agenda. Go first and name it. The aim is honest reordering, not resolution, the recognition that we keep asking God to serve our kingdom while saying the words of his.

objections.objection: A God who insists you praise his name before he will help you sounds like a fragile ego, not a loving Father. Why should the Maker of the universe need me to tell him how great he is before he listens to my problem?
objections.response: Bell grants how it sounds, and the instinct behind it is healthy, because a God who needed our applause to feel secure would not be worth praying to. But hallowing is not for God's sake. It is for ours. God does not gain anything when his name is honored, the way a mountain gains nothing when you admire it. You do. The honoring is not flattery he requires, it is reality the human heart was built to live inside, and a heart that puts anything else first is a heart already cracking on a center that cannot hold its weight. To pray hallowed be your name is to ask God to fix that, to make first in me what is genuinely first in the universe, so that I stop worshiping things that will crush me. He is not fishing for compliments. He is healing the disordered love that is the source of half my misery. The petition is mercy wearing the costume of praise.

objections.objection: Praying your kingdom come and your will be done sounds like passive resignation, like giving up and letting whatever happens happen because it must be God's will. It kills the drive to change anything.
objections.response: It is the opposite, and the words themselves prove it. Your kingdom come is not surrender to the way things are, it is a demand that the way things are be overthrown by the way things ought to be. On earth as it is in heaven means we are praying for a gap to close, between the world as God intends it and the world as it is, which is a profoundly dissatisfied prayer, not a resigned one. The prophets prayed this way, refusing to accept that injustice was simply the weather. To pray your kingdom come is to look at every broken thing and refuse to call it final. Far from killing the drive to change things, it is the engine of it, because you cannot pray for God's kingdom to come and then sit comfortably in the kingdoms of this world. It makes you restless in exactly the right direction.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you are honest, what is actually sitting in the first place in your heart this week, and what would it mean to ask God to put his name there instead?
sessions.practice: This week, before you bring God a single request, spend the first minute of each prayer only on him, his name, his character, the things about him that are true regardless of your circumstances. No asking yet. Just hallowing. Then, when you do bring your requests, pray each one through the question, am I asking God to bless my kingdom or to bring his. Write down what you notice when you put his name first on purpose, and whether your asking changed.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we come to you with our lists, and our lists begin with us, and we have called that normal for so long we no longer see it. Forgive us for the small kingdoms we run badly and defend fiercely, and for asking you to fund them. Hallowed be your name, not because you need our praise but because we need to give it, because our hearts break on every other center. Your kingdom come, even into the places we have been ruling, even at the cost of the throne we have been sitting on. Reorder what we want, until we want you first. On earth as it is in heaven. Amen.
reflection: What is sitting in first place in my heart, and how is that disordered desire surfacing as anxiety, anger, or exhaustion?
What does the small kingdom I run look like, the one where I am king, and what would it cost me to pray for it to be replaced by God's?
Where am I asking God to bless my plans when I should be asking him to give me new ones, his kingdom instead of mine funded?
sessions.teaching: We come to prayer with a list, and if we are honest the list begins with us. Our needs, our fears, our people, our plans, the thing that is keeping us up tonight. That is not wicked, it is human, and Jesus does not condemn it. But watch what he does in the prayer he teaches, because the order is everything. The first three petitions are not about us at all. Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done. Only after God's name, God's reign, and God's will does the prayer turn to our bread, our debts, our temptation. The structure is a deliberate reversal of the order we walk in with, and the first question we have to sit with is why. Why would a Father who, Jesus says a few verses earlier, already knows what we need before we ask, make us ask first for his name to be honored. It can sound, if we are honest, a little like vanity. Take that suspicion at full strength, because it is the honest one. A God who demands to be told how great he is before he will attend to the help we actually came for sounds less like a loving Father and more like a fragile ego, a cosmic insecurity fishing for applause. We know people like that, and we do not enjoy praying to them. Grant the instinct, because the instinct is right about one thing. A God who needed our praise to feel secure would not be worth the breath. But the suspicion misreads what hallowing is for, completely, and getting this right opens the whole prayer. God does not need his name hallowed. You need to hallow it. The honoring adds nothing to God, the way your admiration adds nothing to a mountain and your refusal to admire it subtracts nothing from its height. The hallowing is not for the mountain. It is for the eyes of the one who looks. And here is the truth about the human heart that this petition is built to heal. The heart always crowns something. It always has a first thing, a center it organizes everything else around, and whatever sits in that center is what it actually worships, whatever we call it. For most of us, most of the time, that center is occupied by something that cannot bear the weight, money, or the good opinion of people, or a relationship, or our own control, and a heart built on a center that cannot hold is a heart that is always, quietly, breaking. To pray hallowed be your name is to ask God to do the one thing that heals that. It is to ask him to make first in me what is actually first in reality, to take the throne of my wanting away from the things that crush me and put his own name there, where it belongs and where my heart was built to rest. That is not flattery he requires. It is mercy he extends, the reordering of the disordered love that is the source of half my misery. So the petition is not God demanding praise. It is God offering to fix the human heart at its root. Then comes your kingdom come, and this one is not safe either, though we say it like it is. We hear it as a vague hope for things to get better, ideally along the lines we already prefer. But a kingdom is about a king, about who reigns, and to pray your kingdom come is to pray for a different king than the one currently on the throne of my life, which is, almost always, me. Every one of us runs a small kingdom. We have our domain, our preferences enforced, our will done, and we defend it fiercely and rule it badly. To pray your kingdom come is, quietly, an act of treason against my own reign. It asks God to come and take the throne I have been sitting on. And on earth as it is in heaven tells you the shape of what we are asking, because it names a gap, the distance between the world as God intends it, where his will is done perfectly, joyfully, completely, and the world as it actually is, where it is not. Walter Brueggemann called this the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept that the way things are is simply the way things must be, the holy dissatisfaction that will not call any broken thing final. To pray your kingdom come is not resignation, the passive shrug of whatever will be will be. It is the opposite. It is the most dissatisfied prayer there is, a demand that the gap close, that earth come to look like heaven, and it makes you restless in exactly the right direction, because you cannot honestly pray it and then sit comfortably in the kingdoms of this world. And I have to confess where I break down, because I pray these words and then immediately undercut them. I pray your kingdom come while quietly hoping God will instead fund mine. I pray hallowed be your name and then spend the day building my own. I ask God to bless my plans rather than asking him to replace them with his, which is asking him to be a means to my ends, a chaplain to my kingdom, when the prayer asks for the dismantling of that kingdom altogether. So here is the verdict this session leaves us with. Prayer is not first about getting what I want. It is about being given new wants. It is the slow, daily reordering of a disordered heart, the petition that asks God to take what is first in me and replace it with what is first in him. We come to prayer to change our circumstances. Jesus teaches us a prayer that begins by changing our desires. Hallow his name first, and your wanting starts to heal. Seek his kingdom first, and your small one loosens its grip. Ask for his will on earth as in heaven, and you become, slowly, a person who is no longer at home in the way things are.

scriptureStudy.note: Hallowed be your name. The first petition is about God, not us, and it is not flattery he needs but reordering we need, asking that his name take the first place in us that it already holds in reality.

Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. A kingdom means a king, so this is a prayer for a different reign than our own, and on earth as in heaven names the gap we are asking God to close.

Your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Jesus says this just before the prayer, which means the asking is not to inform God but to form us, to reorder the one praying rather than to update the one prayed to.

Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. The same reordering as the prayer, the kingdom sought first and the needs trusted to follow, desire put in its right order.

One thing have I asked of the Lord, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life. The psalmist models a heart with one first thing, a single ordered desire, which is what hallowing his name slowly produces in us.

Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts, the whole earth is full of his glory. The vision of heaven is the unceasing hallowing of God's name, which is precisely what we ask to spread to earth when we pray hallowed be your name.

The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever. The end of the story is the answer to your kingdom come, the gap finally closed, every rival throne emptied, which is what the petition reaches toward.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up Augustine's account of disordered love, because it is the engine underneath this whole session and it has shaped Christian thinking about desire for sixteen centuries. Augustine argued that sin is not mainly the love of bad things but the disordering of loves otherwise good, loving lesser things more than greater ones, putting created goods where only the Creator belongs. On this account the human problem is not that we want too much but that we want wrongly, that our loves are out of order, and the healing is not the killing of desire but its reordering, learning to love each thing in its proper measure with God first. Set this beside the modern assumption that desire is simply given, that what I want is who I am and ought not be questioned, and ask what is lost when we stop believing our wants can be wrong and can be retrained. A serious group should connect this to James K. A. Smith's argument that we are formed less by what we think than by what we love, and that our loves are shaped by habits and liturgies, including the daily liturgy of prayer, which means praying hallowed be your name is not a sentiment but a practice that slowly reorders the heart. And weigh Brueggemann's prophetic imagination alongside it, the insistence that prayer for God's kingdom is not private piety but a public refusal of the present order, a holy dissatisfaction. The discipline is to see prayer as formation, not information, the long retraining of a disordered heart toward its true and final good, which is God himself first and everything else in him.
