bibliography.title: A Praying Life: Connecting with God in a Distracting World
bibliography.author: Paul E. Miller
bibliography.note: A gentle account of prayer as a child coming to a Father, refusing to make prayer a performance, useful across all five sessions. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Message of the Psalms
bibliography.author: Walter Brueggemann
bibliography.note: Recovers lament as a central and faithful form of prayer and argues that its loss leaves the church unable to tell the truth about suffering. Anchors session 5 on prayer in the dark.

bibliography.title: Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Treats prayer with unusual honesty, including prayer that seems to bounce off the ceiling and the times God feels most absent. Supports session 5 on unanswered prayer. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The source of the distinction between cheap grace and costly grace that grounds session 4, that grace is free but never cheap and that real forgiveness always costs the forgiver. Background for the hinge clause.

bibliography.title: Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity, and Answering God
bibliography.author: Eugene Peterson
bibliography.note: Peterson's writing on prayer and the Psalms as the school of prayer, and against the hurry and self-sufficiency of modern life, informs the account of dependence in session 3. Leader to confirm before stating as the study's position.

bibliography.title: The Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The source of the line that the heart is restless until it rests in God, and of the account of disordered love that stands behind prayer as the reordering of desire. Background for sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: The Lord and His Prayer
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A short exposition of the Lord's Prayer clause by clause, reading it in its first-century Jewish setting and as a prayer for God's kingdom. Useful across the study, especially session 2. Leader to confirm specifics before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit
bibliography.author: James K. A. Smith
bibliography.note: Argues that we are formed by what we love and that our loves are shaped by practices, including the daily practice of prayer, which supports session 2 on prayer as the reordering of desire. Offered as a balancing voice.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the tender heart of Christ toward the weary and the burdened, useful for those for whom the word Father is hard and who need to see God's posture in session 1. Leader to confirm before attributing claims to Bell.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: Traces how the modern self came to imagine itself as buffered and self-contained, sealed off from any sense of being held, which illuminates the resistance to dependence the study names in session 3. Offered as a diagnostic voice, not a devotional one.

bibliography.title: Reflections on the Psalms
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis on the Psalms, including the difficult and the lamenting ones, useful background for the recovery of honest and dark prayer in session 5. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as Bell's own argument.

glossary.definition: The model prayer Jesus gave when his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, recorded in Matthew 6 and Luke 11. The study treats it not as a script to recite but as a school of prayer, walked through one clause at a time.

The act by which God makes those who were not his children into sons and daughters, giving them the right to call him Father. The study grounds the address of the prayer here, so that the fatherless can pray Father not by feeling but by gift.
The Aramaic word for Father that Jesus used and that the Spirit prompts in the adopted, intimate without being irreverent, the near word held together with the holiness of a God in heaven.

The honoring of God's name as holy, the first petition of the prayer, understood in the study not as flattery God needs but as the reordering the human heart needs, putting first in us what is already first in reality.

Augustine's account of sin as loving lesser things more than greater ones, putting created goods where only the Creator belongs. The study reads prayer as the slow reordering of these loves toward God first.

The reign of God, the rule of the true King, which the prayer asks to come on earth as in heaven. To pray your kingdom come is to pray for a different king than oneself and to refuse to call any broken thing final.

The petition for today's basic provision, asked one day at a time with no stockpile, echoing the manna in the wilderness. The study reads it as the confession that we are creatures who do not keep ourselves alive.

The truth that we are made and not self-made, kept in being moment by moment by God, contingent rather than necessary. The study treats the recovery of creatureliness as freedom rather than humiliation.

Bonhoeffer's term for grace that is free but never cheap, that cost God the life of his Son and costs the disciple their life in following, set against cheap grace, forgiveness that demands and absorbs nothing.

The release of the claim to make an offender pay a real debt, the absorbing of a genuine cost by the one who was wronged. The study distinguishes it sharply from denial, from restored trust, and from the abandonment of justice.

The biblical prayer of complaint, protest, and unanswered ache, making up roughly a third of the Psalms, some of which do not resolve. The study recovers it as a faithful form of prayer, not a failure of faith.

The garden where Jesus prayed the night before the cross, asking that the cup pass from him, a prayer the Father did not answer as asked. The study makes it the center of its account of unanswered prayer and persistence.

The keeping-on-asking Jesus commands in the parables of the friend at midnight and the persistent widow, understood not as wearing down a reluctant God but as the refusal of a trusting child to stop coming to the Father.

quoteCards: God is not your father scaled up. God is the Father your father was only a broken copy of.
The first thing prayer does is not change God. It tells you who you are. Child.
Hallowed be your name is not flattery God requires. It is mercy that reorders a heart breaking on the wrong center.
You did not grow the wheat. You did not give yourself the breath to wake. Give us this day our daily bread.
Forgiveness does not say the wound did not matter. It says the debt was real, and chooses to absorb it.
